historical_record.description: The Office of the Assessor-Recorder photographed the property for tax assessment. Embarcadero Cafe, Vic's Naval Uniforms, Sea Cliff Cafe, Emerson Drug Company and Harbor Hotel were at the address.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 90, Ferry Building.
California voters approved a $600,000 bond, repayable from port revenues, to build a union ferry depot in San Francisco.

Construction contracts were let for A. Page Brown's design; Brown died soon after, and from February 1896 Edward R. Swain saw the building through as supervising architect, with the port's chief engineer H. C. Holmes. After litigation over the stone, it was faced in Colusa sandstone from the Sites quarry rather than Oregon gray stone.

Opened to the public. Its 235-foot tower, modeled on the Giralda of Seville Cathedral, carried the largest clock faces in the country, 22 feet across, and the harbor time ball moved here from Telegraph Hill until 1909.
With ferry traffic in decline since the Bay Bridge opened in 1936, the upper-floor waiting rooms were remodeled into offices by William G. Merchant.
Ferry service to the Oakland Mole for rail passengers ended, replaced by buses.
BART trains began running between the East Bay and San Francisco through the tube under the building's south wing.
